title: Airbnb's Air Mattress Beginning
description: This episode traces how two broke roommates turned spare air mattresses into a company worth more than Hilton and Wyndham combined. It establishes the near-failure, the Y Combinator advice that changed everything, and the recession-era conditions that let Airbnb scale into a global business.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: In 2007, two broke roommates in San Francisco put three airbeds on their apartment floor to help pay the rent. That simple idea would eventually become Airbnb, a company now worth more than Hilton and Wyndham Hotels & Resorts combined. The roommates were Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia, both graduates of the Rhode Island School of Design. They were short on cash, and a design conference was about to bring more visitors to San Francisco than the city's hotels could accommodate. So they inflated three airbeds in their apartment, put them online, and called it Air Bed and Breakfast. They weren't trying to build a global company. They just wanted to make enough money to cover the rent. Then three people actually booked. And something unexpected happened. The guests weren't the sketchy backpackers they had imagined. They were ordinary people who were surprisingly comfortable staying in a stranger's home. Some even sent over resumes and LinkedIn profiles to show the hosts they could be trusted. That was the first sign that there might be something bigger here. But almost nobody else saw it. The founders struggled to raise money because investors couldn't understand why anyone would pay to stay in a stranger's home when hotels already existed. By late 2008, Chesky and Gebbia were running out of money and piling up credit-card debt. Then they got into Y Combinator's Winter 2009 batch. The advice was simple: go to your users. Their users were mostly in New York, so Chesky and Gebbia flew there, met hosts face-to-face, helped them improve their listings and pricing, and noticed something important, the photos were terrible. So they rented a camera and photographed the homes themselves. The listings got better, bookings started increasing, and the numbers finally began moving. In February 2009, Airbnb's weekly fees climbed from $460 to $897 to $1,428. For the first time, the founders knew they weren't just surviving. They had found something. And that was the turning point.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It worked because Airbnb wasn't just a beach-house rental. It turned spare rooms, apartments, and even rented studios into income, at exactly the moment the Great Recession was pushing a generation of travelers to look for cheaper alternatives. With third co-founder Nathan Blecharczyk, they built a review system that helped create trust between strangers, and the business kept growing. Today Airbnb lists more than three million places to stay in almost two hundred countries, valued at thirty one billion dollars, and hotel chains that once asked what Airbnb even was are now buying rival home rental companies themselves.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It took two guys almost nobody believed in, an idea investors saw as a lawsuit waiting to happen, and a trip to New York to sit with the strangers actually using the product. That was the breakthrough. That's the story, decoded. Follow for more, and I'll see you in the next one.
